newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian villagers spend days in volcano shelters.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian villagers spend days in volcano shelters.

text.p: Villagers evacuated from the slopes of Indonesia's most active volcano said on Monday they wanted to go home despite further rumblings from Mount Merapi.
"I am not happy at the moment. I want to go home," said Budiyono, one of 2,126 villagers evacuated from the Kaliurang area on Friday after Merapi spewed hot gas, lava and ash.
She said she wanted to return to Kaliurang, with its lush vegetation and cool air, because she was not afraid of eruptions.
"I like living there. My husband and my two children are all living in Kaliurang and life is easy there," she said.

Vulcanologists, wary of the 2,911-metre Merapi since it erupted without warning and killed 60 people in November 1994, said they needed at least two more days to decide whether it was safe for the villagers to go home.
Officials evacuated more than 8,000 people from four districts around the mountain after it intensified its activity last week, spouting hot gas, ash and lava.
Panut, a vulcanology official in Kaliurang, on the mountain's southern slope, said his office remained on alert as tremors continued.
"The volcano's status is still 'alert'. It continued to produce tremors over the past 12 hours. The seismograph went crazy last night," he said on Monday.

A number of villagers have taken refuge at nearby Argo Binangun village, one of the areas designated as a shelter for volcano evacuees. They sleep on mats at three schools, a town hall and the house of the village head.
Refugees said they were bored. Most of them fast during the day in the Moslem holy month of Ramadan, which ends on February 8.
Wiyono, another refugee from Kaliurang, said he was used to the eruptions and wanted to go home as soon as possible.
"I am used to living there. I am used to living in danger. I will move from Kaliurang only if I am forced to do so and only if there is a major eruption," he said.

Merapi, in central Java, overlooks the popular tourist town of Yogyakarta and the ancient Buddhist temple site of Borobodur. The stream of smoke and ash from its summit are clearly visible on clear days.
Its most destructive eruption this century was in 1930, when 1,300 people were killed.
